埃爾克角號具有雄渾而深沉的音色，帶有濃郁的銅管樂器特徵。其音質溫潤厚重，富有穿透: The erke has a full, deep timbre with a strong brass character. The tone is warm and heavy and carries well; in the upper register it takes on a bright metallic sheen, while in the low register it is deep and full. The instrument's range is wide and can cover everything from a low horn call to a piercing high note. Its way of resonating is distinctive: the huge conical tube makes the sound wave resonate strongly and produces a full sound. Compared with the French horn of the modern symphony orchestra, the erke is rougher and more primitive; compared with the traditional trumpet, its sound is heavier and lower. It plays an important part in Andean mountain music, and its distinctive sound carries across the wide high plateau.
埃爾克角號是源自玻利維亞、分布於格蘭查科、智利北部與阿根廷西北部的氣鳴樂器，以唇: The erke is an aerophone that comes from Bolivia and is found in the Gran Chaco, northern Chile and north-western Argentina; it sounds by lip vibration. Its body is joined from two or more lengths of bamboo with the internal nodes removed, the outside is often wound with gut or wool, one end usually carries a cow-horn or brass bell and the other end is blown, and the whole may be three to seven metres long. Andean folk ensembles use it for secular music, while indigenous and Creole communities use it for ritual; traditionally only adult men play it, though it is uncommon, and it is common in winter.

One end normally carries a cow-horn or brass bell and the other end is blown. The instrument is a lip-reed aerophone, but the source does not state the specific material of the lip reed or the mouthpiece, nor the adhesive used at the joints. 埃爾克角號起源於玻利維亞，並見於格蘭查科、智利北部與阿根廷西北部。二十世紀後半葉: The erke comes from Bolivia and is found in the Gran Chaco, northern Chile and north-western Argentina. In the second half of the twentieth century Andean folk music groups took it up for secular music, but among Andean indigenous and Creole communities it is used only for ritual. Traditionally, though not often, only adult men play it, and playing it outside ritual is considered sacrilege. It is mostly blown in winter, because the belief is that playing it in spring or summer brings snow.
